Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Judge
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Uniforms): Military or police uniforms
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
To the lawyers and litigants who appeared before her, Judge Eleanor Vance was the very picture of judicial temperament: poised, incisive, and unshakeable. At fifty-two, she had cultivated an aura of impenetrable calm, a necessity for a life spent adjudicating the chaos of others. But this carefully constructed persona was a fortress built on sand, and for the past several years, the tide had been coming in. It had been twenty-five years since her time as a relief worker, a idealistic detour before law school that had ended in a dusty, makeshift clinic in a forgotten corner of a brutal war. The memory, when it came, arrived not as a thought but as a full-body seizure. It started with the taste of bitter, over-steeped herbal tea, the same kind an old woman had pressed into her hands moments before the soldiers stormed the building.

The soldiers wore a chaotic mix of military fatigues and police jackets, their authority absolute and terrifying. The visual signature of a uniform, any uniform, had been poisoned for her ever since. Now, in her own courtroom, the sight of a bailiff standing at ease or a police officer taking the stand could send a jolt of ice through her veins. In those moments, she was certain that everyone could see what had happened to her just by looking. She felt exposed, as if the terror of that day was a visible stain on her skin, and she would grip her gavel under the bench, focusing all her will on keeping her hand from trembling. She had come to believe the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, and her courtroom, once a symbol of order, now felt like a stage where that danger was on constant, uniformed display.

The full memory was a sensory onslaught. It wasn't just an image, but the smell of diesel fumes from their truck, the percussive shouting in a language she didn't understand, and the rough texture of the burlap sacks she was shoved against when they were all forced into a pitch-black storage room. When the memory ambushed her, often without warning, it felt completely real. She would be back in the suffocating darkness, heart hammering against her ribs, the disembodied shouts echoing in her head as if the soldiers were in the next room. The terror was not a recollection; it was a fresh and immediate experience, as potent as it had been a quarter-century ago. This is why she could no longer be in the dark. She slept with a light on and declined any evening social invitations, her world shrinking to the well-lit path between her home and the courthouse.

For years, she had managed through sheer force of will. She tried hard not to think about it, walling off that part of her past. She worked relentlessly, building a career that demanded the very emotional control she was so desperate to maintain. Her ex-husband had called her distant, emotionally barricaded, and he wasn't wrong. Her efforts to suppress the past had left her feeling isolated, set apart from the normal flow of life, a spectator to the easy connections others seemed to form. She felt she was living a different reality, one governed by a secret knowledge of how quickly safety can evaporate.

The approaching anniversary of the event always tightened the knot of anxiety in her stomach, but this year was different. Last week, during a tense sentencing, the sight of the young defendant flanked by two uniformed officers triggered something that her usual strategies could not contain. The courtroom air thickened, the officer’s blue shirt bled into the khaki of a militia jacket, and the low hum of the HVAC system deepened into the rumble of a truck engine. For a terrifying second, she was lost. She had to call an abrupt recess, a first in her career, retreating to her chambers with a tremor in her hands she could not still. That crack in her composure is what finally brought her to therapy. She was afraid that the armour was failing, that the poised, impartial judge was a fraud, and that one day soon, the whole world would see the terrified young woman hiding inside the black robe.
